beats.say: DeepLogLens. A grounded RAG log intelligence platform, built on an asynchronous Kafka pipeline. We are going to go slowly. One idea at a time. And after every idea, I'll stop and ask you a question, so you know it has stuck before we build the next thing on top of it.
Here's how each topic will go.
First, the problem the piece solves. If you can't say why something exists, you can't defend it.
Then the mechanism, box by box. The actual messages, the actual tables, the actual transaction. We'll fill each diagram in one step at a time.

Then the options you didn't choose. One or two real alternatives for every big decision, and the argument for the one you chose. That's what makes an interviewer believe the design is yours: you know what else you could have done, and why you didn't.
And then a check. A question appears, a ring counts down a few seconds of thinking time, and you answer out loud, with the reason, before the answer appears.
One rule for this whole lecture.
Every sentence you'll hear matches a line on your resume. Your resume is the map. This lecture is the territory behind each phrase on it.
So when an interviewer points at any phrase, idempotent upserts, corrective RAG, per session tables, you'll know the mechanism, the alternatives, and the numbers behind it.
Topic one. The problem. What is DeepLogLens actually for?
Picture the scenario it's built for.
It's three in the morning. Checkout is returning five oh threes. You have a two gigabyte log archive from a dozen services.
And your manager wants three answers. What broke, since when, and how many users were hit.
The naive fix is to paste the logs into a chat model. It fails four separate ways. Volume: two gigabytes is about fifteen million lines. No context window holds that.
Counting. Ask how many five oh threes there were. A language model estimates from what it sees. It doesn't count.
Trust. The answer comes with no line numbers, so nobody can check it.
Cost. You pay to send every minute of logs, to learn about the handful of minutes that matter.

So DeepLogLens gives each job to the tool that's good at it. Code counts every line, exactly. The LLM only explains the minutes that look abnormal. And every claim points at stored evidence, down to the line numbers.

And it was built under three hard constraints. First, the box. Five hundred and twelve megabytes of RAM for the whole service, so a heap of about two hundred and fifty six megabytes. A two gigabyte file can never be loaded.
Second, rate limits. Thirty requests and six thousand tokens per minute, per Groq key, on the free tier.
Third, correctness. Counts have to be exact, a hundred percent, even after a crash and a redelivery.
Remember these three. Bounded memory, rate limits, exactly once effects. They explain almost every box we're about to draw.

Check 1. Why does DeepLogLens never ask the LLM "how many 503s were there?" A, The context window is too small for the question. B, A model estimates from what it sees; deterministic parsers count every line exactly. C, Groq doesn't allow numeric answers. Or D, Counting would cost too many tokens per window.
B. A language model estimates from what it sees. It doesn't count. So every number comes from deterministic parsers that see every line, and the LLM is only asked to explain.
Topic two. Your resume, read as a map of this lecture. Three bullets, and every phrase in them gets its own topic.
Bullet one says what it does. Log intelligence over gigabyte scale archives. It detects anomalies, writes grounded incident reports, and answers questions citing exact log lines.
Deterministic parsers compute all the metrics. That's topic thirteen.

And the LLM runs only on flagged windows, cutting LLM calls by eighty percent. That's the anomaly gate, topic fourteen. On the one gigabyte demo run: forty two thousand two hundred and five calls, instead of two hundred and twenty thousand six hundred and fifty seven. Eighty point nine percent fewer.
Bullet two says how it ingests. Constant heap streaming ingest. Memory doesn't grow with the file. That's topic twelve.
Archives split into window aligned byte ranges, fanned out over Kafka, and read in parallel. Topics six to eight: the pointers, the splitter, the partitions.
Offsets commit after durable writes. Topic nine.

And idempotent upserts turn at least once delivery into exactly once effects. Topics ten and eleven. The content fingerprint primary key. This is the part you said you want to defend best, so we'll go slowest there.
Bullet three is the AI part. Two LangGraph graphs. The ingest time one writes incident stories, with an LLM as judge groundedness loop. Topic nineteen.
The query time one is corrective RAG. Retrieve, grade, rewrite, re retrieve. Topic twenty one.
Over hybrid search: vector plus full text. Topic twenty.
On per session chunk tables, each with its own H N S W and gin index. Topics twenty two and twenty three. Why a new table for every session, and every alternative you could have picked instead.
Check 2. Which resume phrase is the reason a Kafka redelivery never doubles a count? A, Constant-heap streaming ingest. B, Window-aligned byte ranges. C, Idempotent upserts. Or D, Corrective RAG.
C. Idempotent upserts. Kafka can deliver a message more than once. An upsert that's safe to apply twice is what turns at least once delivery into exactly once effects.
Topic three. Eight words. Every later topic uses them, so let's pin them down first.

Eight words, largest container first. A session is one investigation: checkout outage, September the twenty ninth. Remember, each session owns its own chunk table. And a document is one uploaded file in it: app dot log, two gigabytes.
A part is a byte range of a document. Bytes fifteen million to twenty one million, say. It's never copied. It's only pointed at.

A window, which we also call a chunk, is sixty seconds of log lines, stored as one row, with its exact first and last line numbers. And its primary key is a fingerprint of its content. Hold on to that.
A metric is an exact count for one window and one category. API, five xx responses, two hundred and twelve.
And three things the AI produces. A finding is the LLM's explanation of one flagged window. An incident is a group of related findings with a judged story. And the report summarises the session.
Why is the window the centre of everything?
Because the metrics, the anomaly flags, the findings, the search results, and the citations all share the same sixty second window.
So when an answer cites a window, it points at exactly the minute that was counted, flagged, and explained, with its line range. That's what citing exact log lines means.
Check 3. A part and a chunk: what's the difference?

A part is a byte range of the uploaded file, about five megabytes, and it's the unit of parallel work on Kafka. A chunk is one sixty second window of lines, stored as a row in Postgres. One part produces many chunks.
Topic four. The whole system on one board. Then we'll zoom into each box.
Before the board, two golden rules. Everything else follows from them.

One. The user facing request path never does heavy work. Upload returns in milliseconds, and everything expensive happens asynchronously, behind Kafka. Two. Kafka moves facts, blob storage moves bytes, Postgres holds the truth.

Here's the board. The client, the blob store, one application server with the API and the workers, Kafka, the LLM providers, Postgres for data and vectors, LangGraph for root cause and questions, and Redis for chat history. Let's follow one file through it, in seven steps, with the numbers from the one gigabyte demo run.
Upload. The browser sends the file straight to the blob store with a short lived upload link. The API only checks that it arrived. One gigabyte, and the API never held a byte of it.
Split. A splitter reads the file once and cuts it into pieces of about five megabytes, always at a minute boundary. A tiny pointer to each piece goes on Kafka. Two hundred and five pieces.

Parse. Workers take the pieces in parallel, and each reads only its own slice. Eight parsers count errors, five xx responses, latency and SQL failures per minute. Each piece commits in one transaction. Three thousand and nineteen windows, sixty five thousand metric rows.
Detect. Each minute is compared with the rest of the same log, using median based baselines, rare error patterns, and hard rules. A hundred and one of five hundred and ninety one minutes flagged.
Explain. Only the flagged windows go to the LLM, through one Kafka partition per API key. Forty two thousand calls instead of two hundred and twenty thousand.
Root cause. The first LangGraph graph groups findings into incidents, and a judge checks each story against its evidence. Six incidents.
Ask. Questions are answered by the second graph, corrective RAG over hybrid search, citing the exact windows and lines it used.

Check 4. What travels on Kafka in DeepLogLens: the log bytes, or something else? A, The log bytes, compressed. B, Pointers: an ingest request, then byte ranges. C, The parsed metrics. Or D, Embeddings.
B. Pointers. Kafka moves facts: first an ingest request, then one pointer per byte range. The bytes themselves only ever live in blob storage.
Topic five. Getting two gigabytes in, without the API ever holding them.
Here's the upload, as a sequence. Four actors.
The browser asks the API for an upload link, sending the file name and size.

The API signs a presigned URL for exactly one object, valid for fifteen minutes. A presigned URL is signed on the server with the storage credentials, so whoever holds it can upload that one object without ever seeing the credentials.
The browser PUTs the two gigabytes straight into the blob store. Not through the API.
Then the browser calls confirm.
And the API doesn't trust the client's word. It stats the object itself, so the size it records is the real size.
Then it saves the document row and publishes one small pointer to Kafka: the ingest request. We'll open that message up in topic six.
The API answers two oh two accepted, in milliseconds. Golden rule one: the request path did no heavy work.
Three ways to get the file in. Saving it to the server's disk: on Render, the disk is wiped on every deploy, and the API and the workers can't share it.
Streaming it through the API into blob storage works, but every byte passes through the JVM, holding a thread and buffers for minutes, on a five hundred and twelve megabyte box.
Presigned PUT plus confirm. The bytes never touch the API. The blob store does the heavy lifting. And confirm becomes one explicit event to publish.
Your one line argument: on a five hundred and twelve megabyte box, the cheapest byte is the one the API never touches.
Check 5. Why does confirm stat the object instead of trusting the size the browser sent?
Because the client could be wrong, or lying. The server checks the object itself, so the size and existence in Postgres are real, and only then saves the document row and publishes the pointer.
Topic six. Kafka in four words, and then the first message this system ever produces: the ingest request. We'll open it up field by field.
Kafka in four words. A topic is a named, append only log. Reading a record doesn't delete it, so you can replay a topic from the beginning.
A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is ordered. When you produce a record with a key, Kafka hashes the key to pick the partition, so the same key always lands in the same partition.
Every record in a partition has an offset, its position. When a consumer commits an offset, it's saying: I'm done up to here. After a crash, the next owner starts from the last committed offset.
And a consumer group shares the work. Each partition has exactly one owner thread in the group. So the parallelism you get is the smaller of the number of partitions and the number of threads.

Here's pointer number one, the ingest request. The confirm step in the API produces it, right after it saves the document row. Look at the envelope first. Topic: log dot ingest dot requests, six partitions. The key is the session ID. And the partition is the murmur two hash of the key, modulo six.
Inside the value, four fields. Session ID: which investigation. It names the chunk table the rows will land in, and it's also the key.
User ID: who owns it, carried along so every row a worker writes can be traced to its owner.
Document ID: which file. The documents row was saved, as pending, before this record was sent.

And file URL: where the bytes are. That's the whole trick. The message is a claim check. The payload stays in the store that's built for bytes, and the queue carries a ticket that says where to find it.
So about two hundred bytes of JSON stands for a two gigabyte file. And because the key is the session ID, one session's uploads queue up in one partition, in order, handled by one splitter at a time.

Defend it with two alternatives. One: put the bytes themselves on Kafka. The default record limit is one megabyte, so a two gigabyte file is over two thousand records. The broker now stores the whole file, times the replication factor, and every replay ships the bytes again.

Two: a jobs table in Postgres, polled. That's what version one of this project did. Poll every three seconds, with lock leases so two workers don't take the same job. No replay, and no consumer groups. You end up rebuilding Kafka badly.
A pointer on Kafka. Two hundred bytes, replayable, consumer groups share the work, and the bytes stay where they belong.
Your one liner: the queue carries facts. The store that's built for bytes carries the bytes.

Check 6. The ingest request is keyed by the session ID. What does that key decide? A, Which blob bucket the file is read from. B, The partition: one session's requests always land in the same partition, in order. C, The chunk table's primary key. Or D, How many parts the file is split into.
B. The partition. Kafka hashes the session ID, modulo six, so every request for one session lands in the same partition, in order, handled by one splitter thread.
Topic seven. The splitter. It reads the ingest request, streams the file exactly once, and decides where to cut.
Here's a two gigabyte file, about fifteen and a half million lines.

The splitter consumes the ingest request, opens the object as a stream, and reads it exactly once, with a sixty four kilobyte buffer. It counts bytes exactly at every newline, so every offset it remembers is a true byte position in the file. It holds one line and a few counters. Nothing else.
A line is a record start if it begins with a timestamp, ISO eight six oh one or syslog. Stack trace lines, the ones starting with at, have no timestamp, so they're never record starts.

The cut rule. At least five megabytes since the last cut, and this line starts a new minute, and it has a timestamp. Then the part ends exactly at this line's first byte. So a minute, and a stack trace, always stay whole. That's what window aligned means.
Five megabytes is the target size.

Twenty megabytes, four times the target, is a hard cap, still only on a record start, so one runaway minute can't produce a giant part. A file with no timestamps at all is cut every five thousand lines.
Each part becomes a tiny Kafka message: byte start, byte end, and the line number of its first line. We'll open that message in a moment.
And one ordering detail that matters: the total number of parts is saved on the document row before the first part is sent. You'll see why in topic fifteen.
Here it is in code. A record start is a line with a timestamp.
A window boundary is a line whose minute bucket differs from the previous line's.
The main rule: timestamps exist, we're on a minute boundary, and at least the target size has passed.
The safety valve: four times the target, twenty megabytes, cuts anyway, but still only on a record start.
Emit records a half open range: from the part's start, up to but not including this offset. Half open, so neighbouring parts touch exactly, with no gap and no overlap.
And the offset advances by the exact byte length of each line, newline included. That's why every cut is a true byte position.

Check 7. Why does the splitter only cut on a line that has a timestamp? A, Timestamps are always at five megabyte boundaries. B, So a stack trace, whose lines have no timestamp, and a minute are never split across two parts. C, Because ranged GETs need a timestamp. Or D, To keep parts exactly five megabytes.
B. Stack trace lines have no timestamp, so they're never cut points. Every part starts on a new record, in a new minute, so windows and stack traces always stay whole.
Topic eight. The second pointer. One message per part, and every field in it has a job. Then the key, and why it's not just the document ID.

Pointer number two. The splitter produces one of these per part, two hundred and five of them for the one gigabyte demo file. Topic: log dot ingest dot parts, six partitions. And look at the key: document ID, colon, part index. Hold that thought.
Session ID. It names the chunk table the worker will write. And it's validated as a real U U I D before it's ever spliced into SQL.
User ID, carried through, so the writes stay attributable.
Document ID: which file. Together with the part index, it forms the part's natural key.
File URL: where to send the ranged GET. Still a pointer. The worker fetches only its own slice.
Part index, three. Its position, counting from zero. It's in the Kafka key, and in the part marker table.
Total parts, two hundred and five. The completion target, saved on the documents row before part zero is sent, so nobody can declare the file done too early.
Byte start, inclusive. Always the first byte of a timestamped line, in a new minute.
Byte end, exclusive. Half open, so the next part starts at exactly this byte. The ranged GET asks for bytes from start to end minus one.

And first line number. A worker reading from the middle of the file can't know how many lines came before it. So the splitter, which counted them, tells it. That's how citations come out in the original file's line numbers.
About three hundred bytes of JSON, describing five megabytes of log. Everything a worker needs to do its job without asking anyone, and not one byte of the log itself.
Let's watch it happen. One object in blob storage, read once, never copied. We'll zoom into its first thirty megabytes or so: the first six of its two hundred and five parts.
Each grey line is a byte offset where a new minute starts. These are the only places a cut is allowed.
The splitter cuts at the first minute boundary after five megabytes, again and again. Part zero, part one, part two. Each one is just a pair of numbers, a byte start and a byte end.
Each part becomes a pointer, and the key, document ID colon part index, is hashed to pick a partition. Because the part index is in the key, one file's parts spread across all six partitions.
Three consumer threads in the group, each owning two partitions. All three work on the same file at the same time, each reading only its own byte ranges.
Parallelism is the smaller of partitions and threads. And notice we don't need ordering. Parts can finish in any order, because completion is a counter, as you'll see.
Defend the key. Alternative one: key by document ID alone. Then every part of a file hashes to the same partition, which has exactly one owner thread. A two gigabyte file gets no parallelism at all.
Alternative two: no key. The producer spreads records itself, but placement isn't deterministic, so a replayed part can land somewhere else, and reasoning about where a part lives gets harder.
Document ID colon part index. One file spreads over every partition, and the same part always lands in the same place, across retries and replays.
Your line: spread one file across every partition, deterministically. And if they ask about ordering: completion doesn't depend on it.
And defend the split itself. One message per file was the first version. One consumer read the whole thing, kept every window in memory, and did all the work on one thread.
Physical part files: write the file again, in pieces. That doubles the storage I O, and leaves N objects to clean up.

Virtual parts: byte ranges that are never copied, read with ranged GETs. Hadoop and Spark call the same idea input splits, and DeepLogLens adds one rule: never cut inside a record, or inside a minute.
Your line: describe the slice, don't copy it.

Check 8. Why does the part message carry the first line number? A, To verify the ranged GET. B, A worker reading the middle of the file can't count earlier lines; it needs the global number so citations use original line numbers. C, It's the Kafka offset. Or D, To pick the partition.
B. Only the splitter saw the lines before the slice. It passes the global number of the first line, so every chunk's line range, and every citation, uses the original file's line numbers.
Check 9. If the parts topic were keyed by the document ID alone, what would go wrong?
Every part of one file would hash to the same partition, and a partition has exactly one owner thread in the group. So the whole file would be processed on one thread. No parallelism at all.
Topic nine. The other side of the parts topic. How a consumer reads a part, and the one ordering rule that decides whether you lose data or duplicate it.
Every consumer has to choose when it commits the offset. Commit first, then process: if you crash after the commit, the record is never seen again. That's at most once. Work is lost.
Process first, then commit: if you crash after writing but before committing, Kafka redelivers the record. That's at least once. Nothing is lost, but you may see it twice.
So DeepLogLens takes at least once, and makes the write safe to apply twice. That combination gives you exactly once effects.
That's your resume line, word for word. Offsets commit after durable writes, and idempotent upserts turn at least once delivery into exactly once effects.
A trap to avoid in the interview. Never say Kafka gives you exactly once delivery.
Say exactly once effects. Delivery over a network is at least once.

Because a sender can't tell a lost message from a slow one, so it retries, and retries duplicate. Kafka's own exactly once feature covers Kafka to Kafka, inside a Kafka transaction. Our effect is a Postgres write, which can't join that transaction.
The consumer's settings. Auto commit is off, and the ack mode is manual. The offset only moves when the code says so, and the code says so after the database commit.

Max poll records is one. One record per poll, so one slow record can never hold four hundred and ninety nine others hostage. That setting came from a real incident: with the default of five hundred, slow records blew the poll interval and the group kept rebalancing, re delivering the same records forever.
The max poll interval is fifteen minutes: how long one record may take before the group decides this consumer is dead and gives its partitions away.
And three threads locally, two in production, in the group ingest part workers, sharing six partitions.
Now one part, from poll to acknowledgement. Five steps.

Poll one part request: part three of two hundred and five, at offset forty one on partition four. Then the fast path. A cheap select on the part markers table: has this document and part index already been processed? If yes, skip everything. Don't even read the slice. Redeliveries and replays cost one query.

Then the ranged GET, outside any transaction. Only this part's five megabytes come over the network. Lines are capped at sixty four thousand characters, and NUL bytes are replaced, because Postgres text can't store them.

Chunk the lines into sixty second windows, at most two thousand lines or five hundred and twelve kilobytes each. Run the eight parsers on each window, apply the local hard rules, and compute each chunk's S H A two fifty six fingerprint. Still no transaction.
Then one short transaction, which does all the writes as idempotent upserts. Chunks, metrics for the new chunks only, the part marker, and the parsed parts counter.
And only after the commit returns, acknowledge. That's when the offset commits. Then try to finalize, which we'll meet in topic fifteen.
Notice the rule behind that order.
Slow I O outside the transaction. One short transaction for the writes. Then the ack.

Version one learned this the hard way: a transaction wrapped around a minutes long embedding job held one of the pool's few connections the whole time, and the pool ran dry. Short transactions keep the pool free.

Check 10. The worker commits to Postgres, then crashes before acknowledging. What does Kafka do, and why is that fine? A, Nothing: the offset was auto-committed. B, It redelivers the part; the upserts make the second application change nothing. C, It deletes the record. Or D, It sends it to the DLQ.
B. The offset never committed, so Kafka redelivers the part. That's at least once, and it's fine, because the upserts are idempotent: applying the part a second time changes nothing.
Topic ten. Exactly what a part writes, table by table, column by column. Starting with the most important table in the system.
This is the chunk table. One of these is created for every session, named log chunks s, then the session's U U I D. Ten columns. Watch the first one most closely.

Chunk ID. The primary key. It's not a random U U I D. It's a S H A two fifty six fingerprint of the chunk, hex encoded, computed from the document ID, the first line number, and the content itself. Same bytes in, same key out. That one choice is what makes the insert idempotent.
Document ID: which uploaded file the window came from, because a session can hold several.
Time bucket: the minute this window covers. A B tree index serves time range lookups, in three hundredths of a millisecond for a ten minute range.
Line start: the first line, in the original file's numbering. The slice's line, plus the first line number from the message, minus one.
Line end: the last line. Together, they turn a citation into exact log lines.
Content: the raw lines of the window. At most two thousand lines or five hundred and twelve kilobytes, so a very busy minute becomes several chunks with the same time bucket.
Is anomalous: set by the local hard rules at insert. The finalizer adds the session wide statistical flags later.

Embedding: a seven hundred and sixty eight dimensional vector. It's NULL when the row is inserted. The enrichment lane fills it in later, which is topic seventeen. It has an H N S W index for cosine distance.

Content T S V: a generated column. Postgres computes the full text vector once, at insert, and stores it. A gin index sits on it. Storing it matters: computing it per query took over a second; stored, about twenty milliseconds.
Created at: when the row was written.
Here's one real row. The fingerprint, the file, the minute, lines three thousand four hundred and one to four thousand six hundred and ten, the content, flagged anomalous, and no embedding yet.
So three indexes on every chunk table: H N S W on the embedding, gin on the text vector, and a B tree on the time bucket. Per session, H N S W and gin indexed chunk tables. That's your resume phrase.
The second table a part writes: log metrics. The exact numbers. One shared table, with a composite primary key of four columns.
Session ID.
The minute.
The category. API, database, errors, performance, auth, lifecycle, traffic, dependency.
And the metric itself. API five xx, SQL timeouts, and so on. Those four together are the key.

Count. Notice this one is additive. If two chunks contribute to the same minute, a very busy minute, the counts add up. So this upsert, on its own, is not safe to repeat. Remember that. It's exactly why the next topic matters.
Sum and average milliseconds, also additive.
And p ninety five, which keeps the larger value on a merge.
One row: session, nine thirty one, API, five xx, two hundred and twelve.
And this is why counts never come from the LLM. How many five oh threes between nine thirty and nine forty is a SQL query on this table. An index scan, in under a fifth of a millisecond.

And two bookkeeping tables. Ingest parts: one row per finished part, keyed by the natural key, document ID and part index. The fast path reads it before doing any I O, and it's written with insert, on conflict do nothing.

And the documents row, with total parts and parsed parts. Total parts was saved by the splitter before part zero went out. Parsed parts goes up by one, only when the part's row was new. Another idempotent upsert, keyed by a natural key.

Check 11. A chunk row is inserted. Which of its columns is still empty, and who fills it? A, content T S V, filled by a nightly job. B, the embedding, filled later by the enrichment lane. C, line end, filled by the finalizer. Or D, the chunk ID, filled by Postgres.
B. The embedding. It's NULL at insert, and the enrichment lane writes it later. The text vector is generated by Postgres at insert time, and the chunk ID is computed by the worker before the insert.
Check 12. Why is the log metrics upsert, on its own, not safe to repeat?
Because it's additive. On conflict it adds the new count to the old one, so applying the same part twice would double every count. It must only run for chunks that are genuinely new.
So here's the key idea of the whole ingest design.
The chunk ID is the S H A two fifty six of the document ID, the first line number, and the content. Concatenated, then hashed.

It's deterministic. Any delivery of the same part, on any worker, after any restart, computes exactly the same IDs. A random U U I D would mint new IDs on every delivery, and the database couldn't tell a duplicate from a new row.
Let's watch it work. Here's one chunk: the nine thirty one window, lines three thousand four hundred and one to four thousand six hundred and ten.
The worker hashes the document ID, the line start, and the content, and gets a sixty four character fingerprint. That's the primary key.
First delivery. Insert, on conflict on chunk ID, do nothing, returning chunk ID. The row is new, so it's inserted, and returning hands back its ID. One new row.
Now the metrics. They're computed for every chunk, but they're only added for the IDs that returning handed back. This chunk is new, so its two hundred and twelve five xx responses are added.

Now the crash, and the redelivery. The same bytes arrive. Same hash, same key. The insert hits the primary key, does nothing, and returning hands back an empty list. So no metrics are added. Still one row. Still two hundred and twelve, not four hundred and twenty four.
That's the whole idea in one line. Same bytes, same key, same row, counted once.

Now defend the choice against two alternatives. A random U U I D: every redelivery mints new IDs, the database can't recognise the duplicate, and you'd need a separate deduplication table keyed on the delivery.

A positional key, document ID and line start. Honestly, that's also deterministic, and it's smaller. But the ID says nothing about the bytes. If a re ingest produced different content at the same position, say after a parser change, it would look already stored, and you'd silently keep the stale row.

The content fingerprint. Deterministic like the positional key, but it also binds the ID to the exact evidence. A citation points at a chunk ID, and that ID is the hash of the cited bytes, so citations are tamper evident. For a system whose whole promise is grounded, cited answers, that's the argument.
And the technical similarity to name: it's the same idea as git's object IDs. The name of a thing is the hash of the thing. Content addressing.

Four follow ups you should expect on the fingerprint. Collisions? S H A two fifty six has a birthday bound of one in two to the one twenty eight. You'd need around two to the one twenty eight chunks before a collision is even likely. That's not a real risk.
Isn't hashing slow? About five hundred megabytes a second per core. A five megabyte part hashes in about ten milliseconds, next to a parse that takes a couple of seconds.

Couldn't two windows be identical? Every log line carries its own timestamp, so two different minutes never have the same bytes. And the document ID and line start are inside the hash anyway, so even identical text in two files stays two rows.
Why sixty four hex characters? Readable in logs and SQL. If storage ever mattered, thirty two bytes as bytea would halve it.
Check 13. A part is redelivered. Walk the chunk insert: what does the database do, and what does returning give back?
The worker recomputes the same S H A two fifty six keys, so every insert hits the primary key and does nothing. Returning comes back empty, so no metrics are added. The database is exactly as it was.
Check 14. An interviewer asks: why not just key chunks by document ID and line start? Give your argument.

Position is deterministic too, and smaller, and I'd say so. But it says nothing about the bytes. The fingerprint binds the ID to the exact evidence, so a re ingest that produced different content can't hide behind an old key, and every citation is tamper evident. For a grounded, cited system, that's worth thirty two bytes.
